rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says Yusuf puts knowledge before wisdom because its context concerns knowledge of interpretation, while al-Anʿām puts wisdom first because it concerns legislation; al-Burhān gives the same rationale, showing deliberate word order.
rows.anchor: وهذا موطن علم فقدم العلم لذلك، وفي الأنعام موطن تشريع فقدم الحكم لذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the mockers in al-Raʿd committed more than denial, so the stronger warning of punishment fits them; al-Ḥajj mentions deniers only. He cites Malak al-Taʾwīl’s distinction that censure may occur without punishment, unlike punishment itself.
rows.anchor: والمستهزئون أعظم جرماً من المكذبين، لأنهم يجمعون السخرية إلى الكذب فكان الوعيد لهم أشد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hole in the ship was less heinous because it was made to preserve its owners’ property, while killing the boy without an apparent reason was worse; each description suits its act.
rows.anchor: فوصف خرق السفينة بأنه شيءٌ إِمْر، ووصف قتل الغلام بأنه شيء نُكْر

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says nukr is more severe than imr, matching the more serious killing of the boy.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة: النكر أشد من الإمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After ordering battle against Mecca’s aggressors and promising victory, the author reads the reference to repentance by some of them as fitting the close “Knowing, Wise”: God knows the fighting’s implications and its prior decree and wisdom.
rows.anchor: أي: بما في القتال أو طيّ ما جرى من ذلك كله بتقديره السابق أولاً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the Muslims fled at Ḥunayn, impressed by their numbers, “Forgiving, Merciful” consoles them and promises that their flight is forgiven and God will accept their repentance.
rows.anchor: تأنسياً لمن فَرَّ من المسلمين في ذلك اليوم، وبشارة لهم بتوبة الله عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those in Hūd both obstructed God’s path and misled others, with multiplied punishment, so they are “the greatest losers”; al-Naḥl describes those who themselves preferred worldly life and are losers, without that added harm to others.
rows.anchor: فكان الأولون أخسر من الآخرين فجيء لهم باسم التفضيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 2:45 the pronoun and closing return to prayer because the preceding context commands it; in 2:153 the close turns to patience because the following verses discuss martyrdom, trials, and the patient response in 2:156.
rows.anchor: فلما كان السياق في الموطن الأول عن الصلاة، أعاد الضمير عليها وختم الآية بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author connects 4:48’s ending about fabricating a grave sin to the context of Jewish distortions and lies: 4:46 mentions changing words and 4:50 explicitly describes their lies about God. The excerpt introduces the contrast with 4:116 but gives no explanation of that ending.
rows.anchor: في سياق الكلام على افتراءات اليهود وكذبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reads indefinite ḥaqq in 3:112 as killing the prophets without any right or cause whatsoever, intensifying the condemnation; definite al-ḥaqq in 2:61 refers to the recognized category of right.
rows.anchor: فكلمة (حق) ههنا نكرة عامة، وكلمة (الحق) معرّفة معلومة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denunciation is stronger in Āl ʿImrān: it universalizes humiliation with “wherever they are found” and repeats the verb and preposition before poverty; al-Baqara simply joins humiliation and poverty.
rows.anchor: فأعاد الفعل وحرف الجر للزيادة في التوكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author treats al-nabiyyīn in al-Baqara as a plural of paucity and al-anbiyāʾ in Āl ʿImrān as a plural of abundance, underscoring the latter’s greater condemnation.
rows.anchor: ذكر الجمع في آية البقرة بصورة القلة فقال: (ويقتلون النبيين) وذكره في آية آل عمران بصورة الكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author identifies definite al-maʿrūf in 2:234 with the specifically prescribed marriage after a widow’s waiting period; indefinite min maʿrūf in 2:240 means any permitted act, such as marrying, remaining, leaving, or adorning oneself.
rows.anchor: وذكر أن المقصود بـ (المعروف) ههنا الزواج خاصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author argues that 2:234’s waiting language signals waiting until marriage is possible; its definite “known course” and the preposition bi suit marriage as attachment, like the spouses-as-garments image in 2:187. Verse 2:240 mentions neither waiting nor the marriage-eligible end of the term.
rows.anchor: الزواج إلصاق كما قال تعالى: {هُنَّ لِبَاسٌ لَّكُمْ وَأَنْتُمْ لِبَاسٌ لَّهُنَّ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says definite al-kadhib denotes a specific allegation: Israel’s food restrictions, the claim that God has a child, or the pagan rules about livestock.
rows.anchor: فعرف الكذب لأنه مخصص بمسألة معينة وهي زعمهم اتخاذ الله ولداً سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By contrast, indefinite kadhiban is used for general fabrication not limited to one defined allegation, as in claims about revelation and other lies against God.
rows.anchor: فالكذب ههنا عام ولم يخصص بمسألة معينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite “the people” in 23:41 identifies a particular people, Ṣāliḥ’s nation, confirmed by their destruction; the indefinite “a people” in 23:44 is general, since successive generations and messengers are described.
rows.anchor: الأولى في قوم معينين وهم قوم صالح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author notes the formal contrast: al-Aʿrāf has the two divine attributes indefinite, while Fuṣṣilat makes them definite and adds the separating pronoun huwa.
rows.anchor: فقد وردت الصفتان في الأعراف منكَّرتين (سميع عليم) ووردتا في (فصلت) معرّفتين وزيد قبلهما ضمير الفصل
